props.title: Dogs in Space
props.initialSlug: Young punks share chaotic house in 1970s Melbourne

sections.content: Dogs in Space captures the grimy energy of Melbourne's late-70s punk scene through a semi-fictional lens. Michael Hutchence of INXS delivers a raw performance as Sam, leading viewers through a drug-fueled share house existence that echoes similar punk chronicles like Sid and Nancy (1986) and Suburbia (1984). Director Richard Lowenstein crafts a documentary-like atmosphere, letting the camera drift through cramped rooms and chaotic parties while maintaining narrative threads about love, music, and self-destruction.

sections.content: The Australian new wave cinema of the 1980s gave us several raw examinations of youth culture, with Dogs in Space standing alongside Starstruck (1982) and Going Down (1983). These films shared a DIY aesthetic that matched their subject matter, often employing non-professional actors and guerrilla filming techniques. The authenticity comes through in every frame - these aren't Hollywood productions sanitizing counterculture, but intimate portraits from within the scene.

The film's treatment of music scene dynamics influenced later works like What We Do Is Secret (2007) and CBGB (2013), though few matched its immersive approach. Where many music films focus solely on performers, Dogs in Space captures the entire ecosystem - the hangers-on, the groupies, the drug dealers, and the scene kids who made it all possible. sections.content: While Hollywood occasionally flirted with punk aesthetics in films like Repo Man (1984) and Return of the Living Dead (1985), the most vital punk cinema came from regional filmmakers embedded in local scenes. Dogs in Space shares DNA with underground classics like Liquid Sky (1982) and Smithereens (1982) - films that prioritized capturing a moment over conventional storytelling.
